Imagine a village of 512 people. Fields, bakeries, theatres, two banks. Everyone needs two loaves a month; three months without bread, and you die. Now imagine I build it twice, identical, and change one thing: where the money comes from. Then I run each village for ten years, ten times over, and count who still has bread.

In the first village money is what it is for us: it is born when a bank makes a loan, and every coin in your pocket is a coin someone else owes. In the second, everyone receives a fixed income every month — five units — and money that sits idle above a small cushion pays a parking fee: two percent a month simply disappears. Nobody owes anyone for it. That's the whole difference.

I don't switch everything on at once. Bare fields first. Then a government. A theatre. A stock market. Cooperatives. Taxes. One rung at a time, both villages, same rung, and at every rung: who is alive, what does bread cost, what does the government owe.

Bare fields, no government. In the debt village, thirty people are left after ten years (*). There is no work for most of them, without work no money, without money no bread. In the SuMSy village everyone lives: five units a month is a meal. Same fields, same bakers. Only the money.

Add a government: public jobs and a bread allowance for the unemployed. Now everyone lives — and the government borrows about three quarters of what it spends, every month, for ten years. I tried every tax the village could bear. Balance the books, and fourteen people are left. The debt village lives *because* its government goes into debt. And it can never get out: in that village, every coin in circulation is someone's debt.

It does — once. While the new money is still filling up the village, the parking fee brings in little, and the SuMSy government borrows its citizens' savings: about two months of guaranteed income per villager. Then it pays every unit back, in every run (*). A startup cost. One village repays; the other cannot.

Now firms get owners, and shares that trade. Money in the SuMSy village had been spread almost evenly. With shares it gathers — in ten years the gap between the richest tenth and the poorest is as wide as in the debt village (*). The money system is not the whole story. Ownership is the other half. Cooperatives close most of that gap again (*).

Land. In the debt village land sells for about four years of rent. In the SuMSy village, nobody sells — because money melts and land doesn't, so land becomes the thing to hold, and the rare sale goes for a fortune. Silvio Gesell saw this a century ago. The fix is a fee on land, paid out to everyone as a dividend: then land trades again, at the debt village's price, and the gap between rich and poor is the smallest of all three (*).

Then I did something unkind: I made everyone greedy. Spend every surplus, ten loaves at a time, forever. The SuMSy bakeries go bankrupt — and someone reopens one — again, and again, fifty times in ten years (*). And everyone still eats. What it took was two things: prices that move when bread runs short, and a village that starts a new bakery when the last one falls. Money didn't save them. Rules did.

Ten years, ten runs, twelve rungs. What it takes to survive: in the debt village, a government willing to be permanently in debt. In the SuMSy village, an income everyone gets and a fee on idle money that pays for the state — and a fee on land, or the rich end up owning the fields. In both: prices that respond, and taxes that stay off bread — the one tax that killed the village was the tax on bread. And the open questions I can't answer yet: how big a public sector can each money afford (*), and what happens in the ten years when you switch from one money to the other. That's the next simulation.

Everything here is a rule I chose, and every number comes from a run you can repeat: the code, the village and the report are public. I built one village and broke it a hundred ways. The question I'd leave you with isn't which money is better. It's this: every rule of money is a choice someone made. Which of them would you change?
